question:
Patient note:
A 58-year-old woman with a six-year history of biopsy-proven cirrhosis related to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis came to the liver clinic for an unscheduled evaluation because over the preceding two weeks she noted her waistband felt marginally tighter and that when lying flat her lower flanks seemed to curve outward a bit more than usual, although she could still zip her jeans without difficulty and denied any shortness of breath, early satiety, ankle swelling, nausea, vomiting, hematemesis, melena, pruritus, or recent weight change beyond one pound. She remained fully functional at her job as a legal proofreader, completed crossword puzzles nightly, and had no trouble balancing the household budget or recalling remote or recent events; family members had not observed personality change, irritability, purposeless movements, or spells of staring. Her past medical history also included well-controlled hypothyroidism on levothyroxine 75 µg daily and stage 1 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL; she had never consumed alcohol, had no history of viral hepatitis, and did not use herbal preparations. Previous upper endoscopy showed small portal hypertensive gastropathy without varices, and she had never required diuretics, paracentesis, lactulose, rifaximin, or hospitalization for gastrointestinal bleeding or infection. Home medications were levothyroxine, vitamin D3 2000 IU daily, and omega-3 fatty acids; she reported no drug allergies. She walked briskly for thirty minutes each morning, followed a 2 g sodium diet recommended by her dietitian, and had lost 15 lb three years earlier through lifestyle modification; body mass index now measured 27 kg/m². There was no family history of chronic liver disease; her mother had type 2 diabetes and her father died of bladder cancer. She never smoked and denied recreational drug use. At presentation—before any intravenous access or medication—vital signs were temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 128/74 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats/min, respiratory rate 15/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % on room air. She was alert, oriented, conversant, performed serial threes promptly, and spelled “planet” backwards without hesitation. Sclerae were anicteric, conjunctivae pink, and the breath carried no sweet or musty odor. Skin exam revealed three scattered spider angiomata over the upper chest and mild palmar erythema; there were no bruises or xanthomas. Jugular venous pulsation was normal, cardiac auscultation showed a regular rhythm without murmurs, and lungs were clear throughout. Abdominal inspection showed a softly rounded contour with barely perceptible fullness of the lower flanks; the umbilicus remained inverted and the abdominal wall was not tense. Percussion uncovered a narrow crescent of dullness in the dependent right flank that migrated when she rolled leftward, and with one hand exerting firm midline pressure a faint impulse was felt on the contralateral side; bowel sounds were present and the abdomen was nontender. The liver edge was firm, finely nodular, and palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin on deep inspiration; the spleen was not appreciated. Lower extremities were free of edema, and neurologic examination showed brisk, symmetric reflexes, intact coordination, and absence of a flapping tremor after 20 seconds of sustained wrist extension. Point-of-care ultrasonography performed prior to phlebotomy demonstrated a coarse, nodular hepatic surface, patent main portal vein with antegrade flow at 16 cm/s, no portal vein thrombosis, and a thin anechoic stripe of free fluid measuring up to 1.2 cm along the right paracolic gutter; kidneys were normal in size and echogenicity, and no biliary dilation or focal hepatic mass was visualized. Initial laboratory studies drawn immediately thereafter—before any diuretic, albumin, or vitamin K administration—revealed: total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL, serum albumin 4.4 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 34 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 46 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 126 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 138 U/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 17 mg/dL, creatinine 0.92 mg/dL, fasting glucose 104 mg/dL, hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, white blood cell count 5.4 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 142 × 10⁹/L, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 1.42. Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody remained negative, alpha-fetoprotein was 4 ng/mL, ceruloplasmin was normal, and anti-mitochondrial antibody remained positive as on prior testing. A screening electrocardiogram displayed normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min with no ischemic changes, and upright chest radiography demonstrated clear lung fields with mildly elevated hemidiaphragms but no pleural effusions. No therapeutic interventions had yet been instituted at the time these findings were documented.

Question: What is the patient's Child-Pugh Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Child-Pugh score grades five features of cirrhosis from 1 to 3 points each. Using pretreatment findings:
- Total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL (below 2) = 1.
- Albumin 4.4 g/dL (above 3.5) = 1.
- INR 1.42 (below 1.7) = 1.
- Ascites: shifting flank dullness and a thin stripe of free fluid confirm mild, non-tense ascites = 2.
- Hepatic encephalopathy: absent, with normal attention and orientation and no asterixis = 1.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 6 (Child-Pugh class A).
Final answer: 6
